::: {.objectives}
**Learning objectives**

By the end of this session you will be able to:

- explore a dataset and detect duplicated records and missing values;
- select columns and filter rows with square brackets, `which()` and `subset()`, including conditions with `%in%`;
- create, recode and rename variables with `ifelse()` and `cut()`;
- sort data frames with `order()`;
- combine tables with `rbind()`, `cbind()` and `merge()`;
- find, remove and replace missing values;
- summarise data by groups with `aggregate()`;
- distinguish long and wide formats and build a site × species table with `xtabs()`.
:::

# Data management in R

Data management (also called *data wrangling*) includes all the tasks we do to prepare our data before analysing them: exploring, selecting, filtering, creating new variables, sorting, combining tables, dealing with missing values and summarising. In real projects, these tasks usually take much more time than the analysis itself, so it is worth learning to do them well.

In this session we will do all these tasks with **base R**, i.e. with the functions that come with R, without installing any package. In Session 6 we will do **exactly the same tasks** with the `tidyverse`, so that you can compare both approaches.

## Our example dataset

Throughout this session we will use a small vegetation survey. In five plots we recorded the species present, their abundance (number of individuals) and their mean height. Each **row is one species in one plot** (one record), and each **column is a variable**.

```{r data-survey}
survey <- data.frame(
  plot      = c("P1", "P1", "P1", "P2", "P2", "P3", "P3", "P3", "P3",
                "P4", "P4", "P5", "P5", "P5"),
  habitat   = c("forest", "forest", "forest", "shrubland", "shrubland",
                "forest", "forest", "forest", "forest",
                "grassland", "grassland", "shrubland", "shrubland", "shrubland"),
  altitude  = c(1250, 1250, 1250, 980, 980, 1400, 1400, 1400, 1400,
                1600, 1600, 1050, 1050, 1050),
  species   = c("Quercus ilex", "Pinus pinea", "Cistus ladanifer",
                "Cistus ladanifer", "Lavandula stoechas",
                "Quercus ilex", "Pinus sylvestris", "Juniperus oxycedrus", "Cistus ladanifer",
                "Festuca indigesta", "Lavandula stoechas",
                "Cistus ladanifer", "Retama sphaerocarpa", "Lavandula stoechas"),
  abundance = c(12, 5, 30, 45, 18, 8, 15, 4, NA, 60, 7, 38, 9, NA),
  height_cm = c(650, 900, 80, 95, 40, 520, 1100, 210, 70, 25, 35, 100, 180, 45)
)
```

We will also use a second table with some information about each species (its family and growth form), which we will combine with the survey later:

```{r data-traits}
traits <- data.frame(
  species     = c("Quercus ilex", "Pinus pinea", "Pinus sylvestris", "Cistus ladanifer",
                  "Lavandula stoechas", "Juniperus oxycedrus", "Retama sphaerocarpa",
                  "Quercus pyrenaica"),
  family      = c("Fagaceae", "Pinaceae", "Pinaceae", "Cistaceae",
                  "Lamiaceae", "Cupressaceae", "Fabaceae", "Fagaceae"),
  growth_form = c("tree", "tree", "tree", "shrub", "shrub", "shrub", "shrub", "tree")
)
```

::: {.note}
Notice that the two tables do not contain exactly the same species: *Festuca indigesta* appears in the survey but not in `traits`, and *Quercus pyrenaica* appears in `traits` but not in the survey. This is very common in real data, and we will see why it matters when we combine tables.
:::

# Exploring the data

Before modifying a dataset, always explore it. Most data problems (wrong types, typos, missing values, duplicated rows) are detected at this stage.

```{r explore-1}
dim(survey)        # number of rows and columns
names(survey)      # column names
head(survey)       # first 6 rows
str(survey)        # type of each column
summary(survey)    # summary of each column (notice the NAs in abundance)
```

To know which values a variable takes, and how many times each appears, use `unique()` and `table()`:

```{r explore-2}
unique(survey$species)           # species recorded
length(unique(survey$species))   # number of different species
table(survey$habitat)            # number of records (rows) per habitat
table(survey$plot)               # number of records per plot
```

::: {.tip}
**Be careful when interpreting `table()`:** it counts **rows**, not plots. `table(survey$habitat)` tells us how many species records there are in each habitat, not how many plots of each habitat we sampled.
:::

`duplicated()` detects rows that are exact copies of a previous row, a common error when data are typed or copied by hand. Let's create a copy of the survey with a duplicated row to see how it works:

```{r explore-3}
survey_dup <- rbind(survey, survey[3, ])   # add a copy of row 3 at the end
duplicated(survey_dup)                     # the last row is TRUE: it is a duplicate
survey_dup[!duplicated(survey_dup), ]      # keep only the non-duplicated rows
```

# Selecting and filtering data

## Selecting columns

As we saw in Session 2, we can select columns with square brackets `[rows, columns]`, by position or by name, or with `$`:

```{r select-1}
survey[, 4]                           # fourth column (returns a vector)
survey[, c("plot", "species")]        # several columns by name (returns a data frame)
survey$species                        # one column by name
```

Selecting by name is safer than selecting by position: if the order of the columns changes, your code will still select the right ones.

## Filtering rows

To keep only the rows that meet a condition, we write the condition in the rows position. The condition is a **logical vector** (`TRUE`/`FALSE`), and R keeps the rows that are `TRUE`:

```{r filter-1}
survey$habitat == "forest"                 # the logical vector
survey[survey$habitat == "forest", ]       # rows of forest plots
```

Conditions can be combined with `&` (and), `|` (or) and `!` (not):

```{r filter-2}
survey[survey$habitat == "forest" & survey$altitude > 1300, ]      # forest AND above 1300 m
survey[survey$habitat == "grassland" | survey$altitude < 1000, ]   # grassland OR below 1000 m
survey[survey$habitat != "forest", ]                               # NOT forest
```

To check whether the values belong to a set of options, use the operator `%in%`. It is much shorter than writing many conditions with `|`, and very useful to select a list of species:

```{r filter-3}
pines_oaks <- c("Pinus pinea", "Pinus sylvestris", "Quercus ilex")
survey[survey$species %in% pines_oaks, ]
survey[!(survey$species %in% pines_oaks), ]     # all the other species
```

Rows and columns can be selected at the same time:

```{r filter-4}
survey[survey$habitat == "forest", c("plot", "species", "abundance")]
```

## Filtering with missing values: `which()` and `subset()`

Look carefully at what happens when we filter a column that contains `NA`:

```{r filter-na-1}
survey[survey$abundance > 20, ]
```

The rows with `NA` in `abundance` appear as rows full of `NA`. This is because R does not know whether `NA > 20` is `TRUE` or `FALSE`, so the result of the condition is `NA`. There are two easy ways to avoid this problem. The function `which()` returns the **positions** of the `TRUE` values, ignoring the `NA`:

```{r filter-na-2}
survey$abundance > 20
which(survey$abundance > 20)
survey[which(survey$abundance > 20), ]
```

The function `subset()` also ignores rows where the condition is `NA`, and its syntax is easier to read because we do not need to repeat the name of the data frame. The argument `select` chooses the columns:

```{r filter-na-3}
subset(survey, abundance > 20)
subset(survey, abundance > 20, select = c(plot, species, abundance))
subset(survey, habitat == "shrubland", select = -altitude)    # all columns except altitude
```

::: {.tip}
**Key rule:** when the column you filter by contains `NA`, use `which()` inside the brackets or `subset()`. Otherwise you will get rows full of `NA`.
:::

# Creating and modifying variables

## New variables

To create a new column, we assign a value to a column name that does not exist yet. Most operations in R are **vectorised**: they are applied to every element of the column at once.

```{r mutate-1}
survey$height_m <- survey$height_cm / 100          # change units
survey$log_abundance <- log(survey$abundance + 1)  # log-transformation (+1 to avoid log(0))
head(survey)
```

To modify an existing column, we simply assign it a new value, and to delete a column we assign it `NULL`:

```{r mutate-2}
survey$log_abundance <- NULL
names(survey)
```

## Recoding variables with `ifelse()`

`ifelse()` creates a new variable based on a condition. It has three arguments: the condition, the value if `TRUE` and the value if `FALSE`.

```{r recode-1}
survey$dominant <- ifelse(survey$abundance >= 30, "yes", "no")
survey[, c("species", "abundance", "dominant")]
```

Notice that the rows with `NA` in `abundance` also get `NA` in the new variable, which is correct: we cannot know whether those species were dominant.

To convert a numeric variable into classes, the function `cut()` is very useful. The argument `breaks` gives the limits of the classes, and `labels` their names. The result is a factor:

```{r recode-2}
survey$alt_class <- cut(survey$altitude,
                        breaks = c(0, 1000, 1400, 2000),
                        labels = c("low", "mid", "high"))
table(survey$plot, survey$alt_class)
```

By default the intervals include the upper limit, so a plot at exactly 1400 m is classified as `"mid"`.

## Renaming variables

To rename a column, we change the corresponding element of `names()`:

```{r rename-1}
survey_renamed <- survey
names(survey_renamed)[names(survey_renamed) == "height_cm"] <- "height"
names(survey_renamed)
```

# Sorting data

`sort()` sorts the values of a vector, and `order()` returns the **positions** that would sort it. By default both work in increasing order, and `sort()` drops the `NA`s:

```{r sort-1}
w <- c(2, 5, 2, 3, NA, 9, 1)
sort(w)
sort(w, decreasing = TRUE)
sort(w, na.last = TRUE)       # keep the NAs at the end
order(w)                      # the 7th element is the smallest, the 5th (NA) goes last
```

To sort the rows of a data frame we use `order()` inside the brackets:

```{r sort-2}
survey[order(survey$abundance, decreasing = TRUE), c("plot", "species", "abundance")]
```

We can sort by more than one variable. For example, by plot and, within each plot, from the most to the least abundant species (the minus sign reverses the order of a numeric variable):

```{r sort-3}
survey[order(survey$plot, -survey$abundance), c("plot", "species", "abundance")]
```

# Combining data

## Binding rows and columns: `rbind()` and `cbind()`

`rbind()` adds rows and `cbind()` adds columns. With data frames, `rbind()` needs the same column names in both tables, and `cbind()` needs the same number of rows:

```{r bind-1}
new_records <- data.frame(plot = "P6", habitat = "grassland", altitude = 1700,
                          species = "Festuca indigesta", abundance = 52, height_cm = 30,
                          height_m = 0.30, dominant = "yes", alt_class = "high")
survey_extended <- rbind(survey, new_records)
tail(survey_extended, 3)

observer <- rep(c("Team A", "Team B"), times = 7)   # a vector with 14 values, one per row
survey_obs <- cbind(survey, observer)
head(survey_obs, 3)
```

::: {.note}
`cbind()` simply pastes the vector next to the table, assuming that the order of the values matches the order of the rows. If you need to combine two tables using a shared variable (such as the species name), use `merge()` instead.
:::

## Joining tables with `merge()`

`merge()` joins two data frames using a **key**, i.e. a column they have in common. This is how we add the family and growth form of each species to the survey:

```{r merge-1}
survey_traits <- merge(survey, traits, by = "species")
survey_traits[, c("plot", "species", "family", "growth_form")]
nrow(survey_traits)
```

The result has only 13 rows: *Festuca indigesta* has disappeared, because it is not in the `traits` table. By default, `merge()` only keeps the rows whose key appears in **both** tables. The arguments `all.x` and `all` change this behaviour:

```{r merge-2}
# keep all the rows of the first table (x = survey); missing traits are filled with NA
survey_traits_all <- merge(survey, traits, by = "species", all.x = TRUE)
survey_traits_all[survey_traits_all$species == "Festuca indigesta",
                  c("plot", "species", "family", "growth_form")]

# keep all the rows of both tables
full <- merge(survey, traits, by = "species", all = TRUE)
nrow(full)    # 14 records + 1 row for Quercus pyrenaica, which was not in the survey
```

::: {.note}
`merge()` returns the rows sorted by the key (here, alphabetically by species), not in the original order. Use `order()` if you need to sort them again.
:::

# Missing values

Missing values (`NA`) are very common in field data. First, we need to find them:

```{r na-1}
is.na(survey$abundance)            # which values are missing?
sum(is.na(survey$abundance))       # how many? (TRUE counts as 1)
colSums(is.na(survey))             # how many in each column?
survey[is.na(survey$abundance), c("plot", "species", "abundance")]   # which records?
```

Then, we decide what to do with them. Many functions have the argument `na.rm = TRUE` to ignore them in a calculation:

```{r na-2}
mean(survey$abundance)                  # NA
mean(survey$abundance, na.rm = TRUE)    # mean of the known values
```

To remove the rows that contain any `NA`, use `complete.cases()` or `na.omit()`:

```{r na-3}
complete.cases(survey)                  # TRUE for the rows without any NA
survey_complete <- survey[complete.cases(survey), ]
nrow(survey_complete)
nrow(na.omit(survey))                   # the same, in a single step
```

Sometimes we know what the missing value should be and we can replace it. For example, if the field protocol says that an empty cell means that no individuals were found:

```{r na-4}
survey_zero <- survey
survey_zero$abundance[is.na(survey_zero$abundance)] <- 0
survey_zero$abundance
```

::: {.tip}
**Think before removing or replacing `NA`s.** Removing them reduces your sample size, and replacing them with 0 is only correct if a missing value really means "zero". A value that was not measured is not the same as a value of zero.
:::

# Summarising data by groups with `aggregate()`

A very common task is to calculate a statistic for each group: the total abundance per plot, the mean height per habitat, etc. In base R, `aggregate()` does this with a **formula**: `variable ~ group`.

```{r aggregate-1}
aggregate(abundance ~ plot, data = survey, FUN = sum)          # total abundance per plot
aggregate(height_cm ~ habitat, data = survey, FUN = mean)      # mean height per habitat
aggregate(species ~ plot, data = survey, FUN = length)         # number of records per plot
```

We can summarise several variables at once with `cbind()`, and group by several variables with `+`:

```{r aggregate-2}
aggregate(cbind(abundance, height_cm) ~ habitat, data = survey, FUN = mean)
aggregate(abundance ~ habitat + alt_class, data = survey, FUN = sum)
```

::: {.note}
With the formula syntax, `aggregate()` removes the rows with `NA` in any of the variables used **before** calculating. That is why the results above do not return `NA`, but it also means that, when we summarised `abundance` and `height_cm` together, the heights of the two records without abundance were not used either.
:::

In Session 5 we will see another base R function for group summaries, `tapply()`, and in Session 6 the `tidyverse` equivalent, `group_by()` and `summarise()`.

# Reshaping data: wide and long formats

The same data can be organised in two ways:

- **Long format**: one row per observation. Our `survey` is in long format: each row is one species in one plot.
- **Wide format**: one row per sampling unit, and one column per variable or per category. In community ecology, the typical wide format is the **site × species matrix**, with one row per plot and one column per species.

In base R, `xtabs()` builds a site × species table from a long table:

```{r reshape-1}
site_species <- xtabs(abundance ~ plot + species, data = survey)
site_species
```

Combinations that do not appear in the survey (a species not found in a plot) get a 0. Be careful: records with `NA` in `abundance` are removed before building the table, so they also appear as 0.

`t()` transposes a matrix or table, i.e. it swaps rows and columns:

```{r reshape-2}
t(site_species)    # now species are rows and plots are columns
```

::: {.tip}
**Be careful with `t()` and data frames:** `t()` always returns a **matrix**. If you transpose a data frame with columns of different types, every value is converted into text. Use it only with numeric tables.
:::

Base R also has a `reshape()` function to convert between long and wide formats, but its syntax is quite difficult. In Session 6 we will learn `pivot_wider()` and `pivot_longer()`, which are much more intuitive.

# Summary

| Task | Base R |
|:--|:--|
| Explore | `str()`, `summary()`, `head()`, `dim()`, `unique()`, `table()`, `duplicated()` |
| Select columns | `df[, c("a", "b")]`, `df$a` |
| Filter rows | `df[condition, ]`, `df[which(condition), ]`, `subset()` |
| Conditions | comparison operators (`==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`), logical operators (and, or, not) and `%in%` |
| Create or modify variables | `df$new <- ...`, `ifelse()`, `cut()` |
| Delete a column | `df$a <- NULL` |
| Rename | `names(df)[names(df) == "old"] <- "new"` |
| Sort | `sort()`, `df[order(df$a), ]` |
| Combine tables | `rbind()`, `cbind()`, `merge()` (with `all.x`, `all`) |
| Missing values | `is.na()`, `na.rm = TRUE`, `complete.cases()`, `na.omit()` |
| Summarise by groups | `aggregate(y ~ group, data, FUN)` |
| Wide table | `xtabs()`, `t()` |
